title: 12   Falsification & Elimination Rules of \(\wedge\), \(\forall\), \(\leftarrow\)
text:
12.1 Falsification is progress
So how do we make judgments? Let’s begin with judgments in science, what we learned from Popper is typically about falsification. In the next chapter we will switch to verification in computational judgments. Together these will seem like a potent combination but there is a catch. What you will notice is that the sorts of statements that are easily falsified are different from the sorts of statements that are easily verified. It is almost as if the two systems are complementary, because in fact for some judgments there are complementary roles. Logicians call this approach substructural because it is not all the rules at once but instead we start to play and wait for situations to emerge that make further rules necessary and interesting.
After the success of Boltzman in explaining gasses and sound as the movement of molecules it seemed plausible to 19th century scientist that light was the movement of a substance called luminescent ether. Believing this hypothesis, Michelson and Morley set out to measure the speed of light as it move through the ether. They decided to measure the same light at right angles. You can think of a canoe moving in a pond. If you measure its speed forward-and-backwards it will be going faster than it is side-to-side. So whatever the orientation of the experiment, the measurement at right angles should be different. Huge surprise, it was exactly the same! Light it seemed was not moving through a luminescent ether.
Science experiments are nearly always about falsifying a hypothesis. There are simply too many factors that can go wrong or unnoticed influences to think of an experiment as proving a hypothesis. Instead, as Popper suggested, the absence of a falsifying experiment is the best support of a scientific hypothesis. So how do we falsify a hypothesis?
As a caution, we often like to inject a variety of alternative words for falsification such as “refute”, “disprove”, “invalidate”, “negate”, “contradict”, and even “reject”. This are generally identical and here just for the poetic license of us authors. It is a form of mal-practice and computer programs are typically strict about requiring just one word such as false. And yet, I’m hoping you are human reading this and not a chatbot and that you appreciate that I did not want to fall asleep while writing this nor did I want to put you to sleep while reading it. Please don’t falsify my hope.

12.2 Falsifying conjunction \(\wedge\)
The following everyday scenarios are generally judged as fair and reasonable. Why is this?

A job candidate’s application list strengths as “punctual and organized” but they showed up late to the interview. They were judged not to be trusted.
Ice is solid and below \(0^{\circ}C\). You squeeze the bag and it is squishy. It is no longer ice.
Entry requires ID and a ticket. You cannot find your ID and cannot get in.

To gather these examples into one we can use variables to replace the parts that varied and see if we observe a pattern. But first, we need to take a moment to explain how we like to write down logic.

Language limits
The English word “AND” is a bit too generic to make a reliable logical operator. For instance, we might write

12 is positive and even.
Study and you will get good grades.

In the first sentence 12 is given two properties that happen to coexist. This is the way logic thinks of “and”. Meanwhile the second sentence seems to indicate that the first property (studying) is responsible for the second (good grades). If you need further confirmation that something is different about these two uses consider swapping the order.

12 is even and positive. (Meaning unchanged)
You will get good grades and study. (Meaning altered.)

Be aware that logic steps back the options for the meaning of everyday words so that when used confusion is minimized.
In order to introduce logical operators recall from your childhood the notations used for other operators such as addition and multiplication:
\[
\begin{array}{rc}
  & 11\\
  + & 12\\
\hline
  & 23
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rc}
  & 11\\
  * & 12\\
\hline
  & 132
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rc}
\\
-  & 11\\
\hline
   & -11
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rc}
  & \\
0 & \\
\hline
  & 0
\end{array}
\] These last two are not too common but they continue the pattern showing that we could operate by the negative sign on a single input and the the constant 0 is akin to an operator with no inputs. We will use a similar notation to begin explaining our logical operators and later we will adjust this into what is known as “sequent calculus”. When this takes up too much vertical space we can flip the notation horizontally similar to \(11+12=23\), but instead of and \(=\) sign we use our judgment symbols \(P, Q\vdash R\) for example. This is the same symbol we used for judgment and indeed the horizontal dividing line and \(\vdash\) here are place holders for a judgment in some systems be it theoretical (\(\vDash\)), practical (\(\Vdash\)), or computational (\(\vdash\)).


Conjunction Elimination

The proposition “\(P\) and \(Q\)” justifies the proposition \(P\). It also justifies the proposition \(Q\).
Because the word “and” is so necessary in everyday language we prefer to use a symbol like \(\wedge\) (or & or && or even AND) and the word conjoined/conjunction to make it obvious that we are trying to study the logic of “and” not the word as it might be used in common language. So in symbols first we have a “Language rule” \[
\tag{$\wedge$-Language}
\langle conjunction \rangle ::= \langle proposition \rangle \wedge \langle proposition \rangle
\] then we have the rules to use conjunctions: \[
\tag{$\wedge$-Elimination}
\begin{array}{rl}
\text{get}_P    & P \wedge Q \\
\hline
& \phantom{P\wedge}P
\end{array}
\qquad
% \tag{$\wedge$-Elimination}
\begin{array}{rl}
\text{get}_Q    & P \wedge Q \\
\hline
& \phantom{P\wedge}Q
\end{array}
\] Alternative with inline notation we may write this as \(P \wedge Q \vdash P\); similarly, \(P \wedge Q \vdash Q\). The traditional name in mathematics is \(\pi_P\) for \(\text{get}_P\) and \(\pi_Q\) for \(\text{get}_Q\) where \(\pi\) represents “project”, as in to project \(P\wedge Q\) to \(P\). As a diagram we can capture this rule thus:
graph LR
    PANDQ["P∧Q"] -->|get_P| P
    PANDQ -->|get_Q| Q







NoteElimination Rules



The term elimination is to signify that we had a premise with the symbol, in this case \(\wedge\), but that symbol has been eliminated in the conclusion. Indeed \(\wedge\) does not appear to the right of the judgment turnstile \(\vdash\) in the \(\wedge\)-eliminiation rule.
As a diagram you can typically spot elimination rules as the arrows that leave the term being eliminated. In this case the arrows leave \(P\wedge Q\) and point to \(P\) and \(Q\). We will see this pattern again with other elimination rules.


Now each of the above sample sentences use conjunction in its own way.

Let us consider the first judgment in practice (\(\Vdash\)):

A job candidate’s application list strengths as “punctual and organized” but they showed up late to the interview. They were judged not to be trusted.

Setting

\(P\) = “punctual”
\(Q\) = “organized”
\(P\wedge Q\) = “punctual and organized” is hypothesized as valid.
\(P\) is false, (the candidate was late).

This means the interview panel can use \(\wedge\)-elimination to justify the claim that the candidate is punctual. \[
P\wedge Q \Vdash P
\] Together we have \(P\) is both valid and invalid.
This is acceptable in a practical judgment where truth can be on a spectrum or have degrees of truth. This would however down grade that degree which prior to the late arrival would have been fully true. This would put the panel in the position to ask for an explanation or institute a probationary period to see if the the punctuality claim gains or looses credence.

Recall that one of the models for practical judgment is to invent a symbol \(+\) that stands between truth \(\top\) and falsity \(\bot\). Once more borrowing from childhood remember those addition and multiplication tables where row \(i\) and column \(j\) has the value of \(i+j\) or \(i*j\), or now the judgment \(i\wedge j\). Here is one of those choices set along side \(\min\) as a numerical representation of the same logic.

\[
\begin{array}{|c|ccc|}
\hline
  \wedge & \bot & + & \top \\
\hline
\top & \bot & + & \top \\
+ & \bot & + & + \\
\bot & \bot & \bot & \bot \\
\hline
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{|c|ccc|}
\hline
  \min & -1 & 0 & 1 \\
\hline
1 & -1 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\
-1 & -1 & -1 & -1 \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]

The truth tables serve a stronger function than we currently need. All we require is that \(P\wedge Q\Vdash P\) and \(P\wedge Q\Vdash Q\), which we read by observing the places where \(P\wedge Q\) in the table are \(\top\). In the small case there is exactly 1, when both \(P\) and \(Q\) are \(\top\) and so indeed both rules are supported. However these tables now hint at mixed facts. For example, if we think of \(+\) as a mix of true and false (the paradox setting) then when we have \(P\wedge Q\) as a \(+\) it could come form having each of \(P\) and \(Q\) at least \(+\). Which makes sense in some logics which might argue that there is a part of each that is true in the mix in those cases and so that should persist. We call this an optimistic view. A pessimistic view might prefer that once there is some doubt the doubt should grow. In any case, this connection to decimal numbers generalizes to large practical judgments where it is too much to write and remember a table. For example in the fuzzy context where truth values are a spectrum of \(a\leq \varepsilon \leq b\) of decimal numbers (possibly allowing \(a=-\infty\) and \(b=\infty\)) we can use the minimum function.

Assuming every proposition \(P\) is assigned a value \(a\leq |P|\leq b\). Choose a tolerance \(a\leq \varepsilon \leq b\) and say that \(P\) is valid (in the implicit context \(\Gamma\)) whenever \(|P|>\varepsilon\), writing \(\Vdash P\). Then the conjunction operator \(\wedge\) can be defined as \[
|P\wedge Q| = \min(|P|, |Q|)
\] Hence, whenever \(P\wedge Q\) is valid then \(P\) is valid, i.e., \(P\wedge Q\Vdash P\). Similarly, \(P\wedge Q\Vdash Q\).

Proof. Suppose \(P\wedge Q\) is valid. That means \[
\varepsilon < \min(|P|,|Q|)\leq |P| \text{ implies } \varepsilon < |P|.
\] So \(P\wedge Q \Vdash P\). Similarly, \(P\wedge Q \Vdash Q\). \(\Box\)

Next compare the judgment in theory (\(\vDash\)):

Ice is solid and below \(0^{\circ}C\). You squeeze the bag and it is squishy. It is no longer ice.

Here the context is theoretical \((\vDash)\) since concepts like solid and below \(0^{\circ}C\) are theoretical/scientific concepts. So we have

\(P\) = “solid”
\(Q\) = “below \(0^{\circ}C\)”
\(P\wedge Q\) = “solid and below \(0^{\circ}C\)” is hypothesized as valid.
\(P\) is false, (the ice is squishy).

We can use \(\wedge\)-elimination to justify the claim that the ice is solid. \[
P\wedge Q \vDash P
\] So \(P\) is again both true and false. However, in a theoretical judgment \(P\) we reject the mixing of truth and falsity. Therefore one of the premises must be false.

Because theoretical logic is based on the hypothesis that all judgments are exclusively true \(\top\) or false \(\bot\) we can reduce the table of minimums to just \(\pm 1\) to obtain the following “truth table” for theoretical conjunction.

\[
\begin{array}{|c|ccc|}
\hline
  \wedge & \bot & \top \\
\hline
\top & \bot & \top \\
\bot & \bot & \bot \\
\hline
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{|c|cc|}
\hline
  \min & -1 & 1 \\
\hline
1 & -1 & 1 \\
-1 & -1 & -1 \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]

Tables like these are known as “Boolean algebra” after George Boole who emphasized the study of strictly true/false logic. Today it is part of greater study of both algebra and logic. Just as learning arithmetic is more than memorizing addition tables, learning conjunction today should be more than memorizing any one of these tables.

Finally let us consider the third judgment in computation (\(\vdash\)):

Entry requires ID and a ticket. You cannot find your ID and cannot get in.

Setting:

\(P\) = “ID”
\(Q\) = “ticket”
\(P\wedge Q\) = “ID and ticket” is required for entry.
\(P\) is unknown (the ID is missing).

Under what logic can the gate agent refuse entry? Well if we are found inside the venue then \(P\wedge Q\) is judged true by the venue rule. Then by the \(\wedge\)-elimination we would have evidence also for \(P\). This could get the agent in trouble since the agent never saw ID and that judgment would not be in question. Of course in theory you likely do have ID, but in a computational judgment evidence is required to justify claims.

Since computational logic involves evidence it is often the case that we could write this with a physical program. The syntax is to have function that extracts from the evidence for \(P\wedge Q\) some evidence for \(P\). A common name for such a function getP though you may also find names like toP or simply .P. We will so more on this when we get to data types but some examples in software might appear as follows:

PythonC++LispIdris


evidence = ("Hello World", 541) 
print(evidence[0])  # prints "Hello World"
print(evidence[1])  # prints 541


struct IntOrString {
    std::string theString;
    int myInt;
};

evidence = IntOrString{"Hello World", 541};
cout << evidence.theString; // prints "Hello World"
cout << evidence.myInt;     // prints 541


Sometimes the methods used by a language are from historic or cultural reasons. In Lisp the data structure is a list and the first element is called the car and the second element is called the cadr. So we can write:
(defparameter evidence (list "Hello World" 541))
car evidence  ; => "Hello World"
cadr evidence ; => 541


Some languages use conversational terms like “where” and “let” instead of brackets or punctuation.
evidence = ("Hello World", 541)
getInt : (String, Int) -> Int
getInt x = i where x=(_, i)

-- alternative is to use pattern matching
getString : (String, Int) -> String
getString (s,_) = s



Now it is not that computation cannot handle tables of truth values, it is simply that when we write them we have to leave some values empty.


Experimental conjunction tablesComputational conjunction tables


In scientific experiments there is no truth, just failure to falsify. So conjunction in experimental values is a form false \(\bot\) and unknown \(?\).
\[
\begin{array}{|c|ccc|}
\hline
  \wedge & \bot & ? \\
\hline
? & \bot & \bot \text{ or }? \\
\bot & \bot & \bot \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]


In computation validity is presence of evidence (data) \(\top\) and when it is missing we leave a \(?\). \[
\begin{array}{|c|ccc|}
\hline
  \wedge & ? & \top \\
\hline
\top & \top \text{ or }? & \top \\
? & \top \text{ or }? & \top \text{ or }? \\
\hline
\end{array}
\]



Said another way, both operators are partial, they do not provide a value for all combinations of inputs so we are left to wonder which of the possible values is intended. In particular we cannot simply assign the unknown to the missing value of truth or falsity can treat this a version of Boolean algebra.

12.4 Falsifying implication \(\to\)
Let us run through a number of arguments which in most contexts would be judged as valid, then we will explain why that is.

Your e-mail provider’s rules say that “If the file is over 5 MB then it will be sent as a link.” You attach a video that is 100 MB; so, your recipient only got a link to the video.
If there is an unsaved file then the application will not close. You close the application with no unsaved work and the application closes.
If you are logged in to the University Wifi then you can access the library databases. You logged in but you currently cannot access the library databases. Obviously you were misinformed.
There will be a school closure, if the authorities predict a snowstorm. The school is closed, but there was no snowstorm, it was a holiday.
If drop a heavier object then it will hit the ground first. Galileo dropped objects of different weight and they hit the ground at the same time.

So let us set aside disjunction and look for other arguments that like conjunction seem straightforward.

The proposition “\(P\) implies \(Q\)” justifies the proposition \(Q\) if we also have the proposition \(P\). We use the symbol \(\to\) (or if <this> then <that> or \(\Rightarrow\)) and write the rule as \[
\tag{$\to$-Elim.}
\begin{array}{rl}
    & P \to Q \\
@    & P \\    
\hline
& \phantom{P\to}Q
\end{array}
\] Historically this is known as modus ponens (the way that affirms). The term elimination however helps us see the parallels with other logic like \(\wedge\).

In many ways \(P\to Q\) is already a diagram, however, it provokes a followup question which is that some proposition \(R\) is surely responsible for \(P\) so if we include this into the picture may get a clarifying diagram.
graph RL
    P -->|f| Q
    R -->|g| P
    R -->|fg| Q
The intention of this diagram is that any two paths between two nodes are equivalent. That is we can go from \(R\) to \(P\) and then to \(Q\) or we may take the shortcut \(R\) directly to \(Q\). This is known as a commutative diagram. We will have much more on this in the next chapter.
To falsify an implication we need only find \(P\) valid with \(Q\) invalid.

Using theoretical judgment (\(\vDash\)) we can falsify the following implication:

If \(n\) is an integer then \(-n\neq n\).

Setting \(P\) to be “\(n\) is an integer” and \(Q\) to be “\(-n\neq n\)”. We can falsify by find an integer, e.g. \(n=0\), and then validating \(-n=n\), or rather, that \(Q\) is invalid. By \(\to\)-elimination (Modus Ponens) the validity of \(P\) proves the validity of \(Q\). \(P\) valid and \(Q\) invalid. In a theoretical logic \(Q\) cannot be both true and false. So one of our premises must be false.


In a practical judgment (\(\Vdash\)) we can falsify the following implication:

If you are logged in to the University Wifi then you can access the library databases. You logged in but you currently cannot access the library databases.

Here \(P\) is “logged in to the University Wifi” and \(Q\) is “can access the library databases”. We can falsify proposition that \(P\to Q\) by observation is \(Q\) is invalid.
Now in a practical judgment it is possible that \(Q\) is both valid and invalid. So this alone does not fully falsify the implication but it suggests further investigation. In fact we can all imagine that from the perspective of the application we do have access but some other unknown practical issue prevents it from succeeding. This is why practical judgments are often much more difficult but also much more representative of events.


Finally let us attempt to falsify an implication in a computational judgment (\(\vdash\)), this time in a scientific context:

If drop a heavier object then it will hit the ground first. Galileo dropped objects of different weight and they hit the ground at the same time.

So \(P\) is “drop a heavier object” and \(Q\) is “it will hit the ground first”. Galileo had \(P\) valid with \(Q\) false. He therefore had evidence for both. Yet, if there was evidence for \(P\to Q\) then with \(\to\)-elimination we would have evidence for \(Q\) being true. In computational judgment true and false cannot coexist. So the only premise without evidence, that \(P\to Q\), must be falsified.

Since computational implication involves evidence we can package that evidence as data and build programs.






Warningif-then is inductive logic not implicational



You might think at first that I mean the standard if-then statement found all over programming languages. I do not. Those behave much more like a theoretical judgment of implication where if expects to be followed by value true if it is to execute what follows the then, e.g.
if closing then saveFiles()
However there are many clues as to why that idiom of programming has nothing really to do with implication. Notice that what follows is an event or task, not a judgment. It may or may not involve data. This construct it turns out is much better understood as a short form of cases. Some readers may infact be familiar with case-switching idioms in programs and how these list multiple options having nothing to do with true and false. It is too late to rename this idiom and many find it useful. So use it. Even so make space for the following interpretation to fill out your computational judgment of implication.


Computational implications are literal functions transforming the evidence we have for \(P\) into evidence for \(Q\). This is why I choose the name \(@\) for the elimination rule. We can think of the evidence \(f:P\to Q\) as describing the function (via substitution or combinators) and when we get evidence \(c\) for \(P\) we plug that into our function \(f\) to produce evidence for \(Q\). Programs often choose suggestive names for function precisely to capture this intent when reading a function application outloud.

PythonC, Java, C++LispIdris


def asString(i) :
    result = str(i)
    return result

print(asString(541))  # prints "541"


String asString(int i) {
    return "" + i;
}

Note that in Java the built-in method toString() already exists for this task, so we have rename it to asString() to avoid confusion. In C++ we can use the std::to_string() method.


(defun toString (i)
  (format nil "~a" i))


The notation in the language Idris and others in the Haskell family make the notation of functions precisely aligned with the logical implication notation underscoring this connection.
toString : Int -> String
toString i = show i

12.5 Putting it together
Notice elimination rules as diagrams are arrow out of the term being eliminated.
Falsification rarely comes with just one step. Often we have to knit together multiple judgments and the part that fails can often be deceptively buried or even missattributed. Falsifications may seem easier because they often just need examples, but because the complexity can be hidden in how many steps are involved and what precisely fails. To offer just a small taste we consider the following example from the family of diagnostics

A common use of falsification is diagnostics where we assemble a list of conjoined statements (propositions) and we find one that is false.

Proposition: A healthy dog’s nose is cold and wet.
Evidence: Your dogs nose is dry.

Conclusions The dog is not healthy.
To take the argument apart we really have the structure of one event implying other:
graph LR
Healthy[Dog is healthy] --> Cold[Dog's nose is cold]
Healthy --> Both[Dog's nose is cold and wet]
Healthy[Dog is healthy] --> Wet[Dog's nose is wet]
Both --> Cold
Both --> Wet
Notice that what is actually been falsified is not any of the premises given but rather the one that could first derive from the others. That is we first have to compose the implication Healthy \(\to\) (Cold \(\wedge\) Wet) with the rule Cold \(\wedge\) Wet \(\to\) Cold to get a new premise Healthy \(\to\) Cold. Finally we find evidence that Cold is false which falsifies either claim that Healthy leads to Cold or that Healthy is true. We can see within each modification of the argument there is room for error and confusion. If this is in a practical judgment we may very well have mounting errors in our conclusions.

So what is missing from all this discussion is how precisely we come to have a claim of conjunction, implication, or universal quantification. By focussing on what is easy to refute we just needed to know how claims could be used, thus eliminated. In the next chapter we flip the script and focus on what is easy verify.

title: 19  How to make a type of data
text:
When we developed structural logic we depended on three ingredients: Language to tell us how to communicate the logic, Introduction rules to tell us how the logic may arise, and Elimination rules to tell us how to draw conclusions. Now as we move to more complex reasoning we find ourselves in confusion as multiple contexts compete for the meaning of our variables. So we need to put up makers that separate context and allow them to coevolve in our reasoning. The simplest tool for this is known as a type and to make one we may actually get rid of push to include data.

Formation the rules we need in place to declare a type, think of this as introduction rules not of proposition but for types.
Introduction the rules we need to introduce data into a type.
Elimination the rules we need to eliminate data from a type.
Computations the rules we need to convert the introduction information it elimination information.

27.2 Pattern Matching
The allegory of sending a file is an archetype of a form of reasoning we all face in everyday life but which presents several challenges to computation. While we would like to think of the file as one piece of data, its creation and its uses are spread apart, often separated by time and space. The separation means that the data will need a number of intermediate uses. We have already seen how we make a data type that breaks down into parts, an “Inductive Type”. This is like the letter writer Dada. There are prescribe number of ways to make the data (introduction rules)
\(\text{case }1: A^{d_1}\to A\) \(\text{case }2: A^{d_2}\to A\),…, \(\text{case }m: A^{d_m}\to A\)
We can shorten this one one function
\(\text{combined case}: A^{d_1}\sqcup A^{d_2}\sqcup \cdots\sqcup A^{d_m}\to A\)
There is only one way to use this data: match each pattern of introduction (construction) and give each of those a role.

title: 16   Quantifiers
text:
16.1 The Universal Quantifier \(\forall\)
\(\forall\), \(\exists\), \(=\), and \(!^n\)
Once more we can look to natural language to get a hint about what logical operators we will find useful. Think of giving out the same instruction to an ever growing list of employees:
There a number of disadvantages to this approach. For one thing we are letting natural language get away with some imprecise form. Notice there is only one use of the word AND yet the Language of AND works in pairs <this> AND <that>. So the proper form would need us to pair up the instructions for which we invent parentheses
Of course this is one of many ways we could pair up the AND’s without actually making the logic any easier to explain.
Since logic is invented by humans for human, it makes sense to create a version of AND which is much more forgiving about repeated use. This would allow us to get the idea into a precise language we could use in reasoning and making future programs. What should this “repeated AND” be called? Pause to think of how you might say the instructions in simpler way. Here are some options that come to my mind.

title: 16   Quantifiers
text:
Language of For All

The grammar of a universal quantifier is given by \[
\tag{$L_{\forall}$}
\langle universal\rangle ::= \forall \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
\] In words we say “For all \(x\), \(P(x)\) is valid” where \(x\) is a variable and \(P(x)\) is a predicate. Variations include “\(P(x)\) holds, for all \(x\)” and “for every \(x\), \(P(x)\) is valid”.

Notice this is another example of binding a variable. So just as with substitution rules and the Paradox of the trapped variable, we need to be careful to rename \(x\) when substituting.

Proposition 1. \(\forall n.(n<n+1)\).
Here the variable is \(n\) and the predicate is \(n<n+1\).
It is not necessary that the predicate actually depend on the variable, for example
Proposition 2. \(\forall n. (2+2=4)\).



Elimination of For All
We have not forgotten how to spell LIE but we are skipping ahead to the elimination rule because this is what truly organizes what “for all” does. When the manager asserts that “All employees wash their hands!” the meaning is found by applying this claim to any single employee. For example this means “Brenda must wash her hands!” And a new employee “Henri must wash his hands!” Notice the application no longer features “All” nor a variable “employee”. Thus it is an elimination of the structure of the operator.

\[
\tag{$E_{\forall}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\\ \Gamma & \vdash c \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash P(c)\end{array}
\]
In words:

If context \(\Gamma\) leads to “For all x, P(x) is valid” and context also leads to a value c for x, then P(c) must hold in \(\Gamma\).”




Introduction Rule for universal quantifiers
Now that we know how to use the “for all” operator we can guess what we need to know to discover an example of a “for all” operator. Basically we need to reverse what we want as a conclusion. We need to know that if context can make a constant value c for x lead to P(c) being valid, then context is saying P(x) is valid “for all x”. This is quite similar to turning a substitution into a function by function abstraction. The major difference is that instead of a function that output data we think of universal quantifiers and proving a proposition.

\[
\tag{$I_{\forall}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\end{array}
\]
In software, a universal quantifier uses a computational judgement, hence evidence (data) must be produced for each \(P(x)\). In other words \(\forall x.P(x)\) in a Brouwerian judgment is synonymous with a function \(x\mapsto P\).

Notice the premise now has an unknown constant c which together with context leads to P(c). How do we come up with that? We do that through a mix of assumption (hypothesis, axioms, laws) and proofs. For example, a manager or a health inspector make a rule that all employees must wash their hands. Can they really know that this has always been obeyed? Perhaps not but in theory that is how it should work. Once we begin to work in practice or in computation we might find we need to relax our rules. We saw this already with AND where we derived new logic based on include partial truths. We can do the same with “for all” but in order that we call something a “for all” we should keep at least on feature that the theory exhibits. And that is the elimination rule.
For example, if we relax to accept that perhaps some employee neglects to wash their hands we should be within our rights to fire the employee and the health inspector can close the restaurant. When it comes to “for all” it is must important to protect the outcome that clean hands handle food than it is to protect the way introduce the law.

16.2 Existential Quantifier \(\exists\)

Language of existential quantifier

The grammar of an existential quantifier is given by \[
\tag{$L_{\exists}$}
\langle existential\rangle ::= \exists \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
\] In words we say “There exists an \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid” where \(x\) is a variable and \(P(x)\) is a predicate. Variations include “\(P(x)\) holds, for some \(x\)” and “there is at least one \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid”.



Introduction rule for existential quantifiers

\[
\tag{$I_{\exists}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\end{array}
\]



Elimination rule for existential quantifiers

\[
\tag{$E_{\exists}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\\ \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash Q\end{array}
\] In words:
> If context \(\Gamma\) leads to “There exists an x such that P(x) is valid” and context also leads to a value c for x, then P(c) must hold in \(\Gamma\) and hence Q must hold in \(\Gamma\).

text:
16.4 Counting quantifiers and uniqueness
In affine logic we remove the option to duplicate assumptions as this can related to physical resources. In the stricter linear logic we further require the use of every assumption.

$! x.P(x) $ means “there exists exactly one x such that P(x) is valid”. This is a counting quantifier. It can be expressed in terms of the existential and universal quantifiers as follows:


In a classical logic, the uniqueness quantifier can be expressed as follows: \[
\exists ! x.P(x) \equiv \exists x.(P(x) \wedge \forall y.(P(y) \Rightarrow x=y))
\] In words, “there exists exactly one \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid” is equivalent to “there exists an \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid and for all \(y\), if \(P(y)\) is valid then \(y\) must be equal to \(x\)”.


Linear and Affine Logics
Meanwhile a rule like contraction clearly seems suspect in concepts like “have a USB port” or “have an egg” where counting seems crucial for the logic. A logic that cares about such counting is often called a “linear logic” (if it needs an exact match) or an “affine logic” (if it is upper bounded by a count). You can find in programming languages like Idris and Rust that allow for these logics. They are especially useful when we care to track that all our files are and memory are used and released as expected, and to boost the security guarantees of vulnerable software. It is hard to ease drop on data if you can only read it once.

The following Idris code shows how to specify that a value can only be used once. Hence the following fails because it used the value hasUSB twice because the preceeding number 1 instruct Idris to use that value exactly once.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner) -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB = hasUSB && hasUSB 
It also fails if you do not use the value at all.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner) 
                    -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB = false 
Idris is only happy if you use the inputs exactly once, so you need to give it to options. Each gets used exactly once and captures the idea of our logic.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner,
                  1 hasOtherUSB : PortScanner)
                  -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB hasOtherUSB = 
                    hasUSB && hasOtherUSB


Rust makes a similar idea practical with ownership. A value once used transfer ownership and in effect disappears and cannot be reused. This is why the following could would fail.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");
send_to_captain(data);
// Next line causes error; data moved.
send_to_criminal(data); 
Here is a safe use of data.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");
send_to_captain(data);
// Next line causes error; data moved.
send_to_criminal(data); 
Unlike Idris, Rust does not require you to use the value.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");  
// data never used, but that's ok

Though nothing should stop you from learning languages like Idris and Rust, this article should convince you firstly of valuable uses for different than expected logic. When your situation demands you can involve future study and coding assistants to select the programming language that supports your logic best.

Counting quantifiers

17.1 Necessary \(\Box\) & Possibly \(\diamond\)
Ever go into the setting of an app and flip a bunch of toggles  and  to customize the behavior of the app? You can even configure this book. And when you do you are engaging with a new kind of logic. A logic uniquely of the 20th century (though the ideas of course are found everywhere in history). It is called modal logic.
The logical operator \(\wedge,\vee, \neg, \forall, \exists\) have experienced nearly 200 years of use and have had time to seep into mathematics. In fact mathematics is somewhat unaware of most of the logical operators have been invented in the last century preferring to contrive all situations into tortured exhibitions of those symbols alone—a project known as “Logicism” which was shown to be impossible in the 1930s. But we are not mathematicians, we are mathematicians that want to compute and the means we will pay attention to progress in the rest of the world of logic. Of the many topics that have had substantial gain for logic arguably Modal Logic has been the most important. This is a logic that admits that reasoning often depends on the mode in which we find the question. Change the mode and you change the reasoning. The two major operators we will survey from this form of logic are obvious to natural language: necessary \(\Box\) and possible \(\diamond\).
I love this type of logic but every video I ever made about it pales when compared to Attic Philosophy. So we are in for a treat today as we watch a true expert bring us the goods.
The basic of “necessary” is to clarify if a claim is true in all modes. This might sound like a variation on \(\forall\) except that unlike \(\forall\), “necessary” \(\Box\) does not depend on a variable. It rather qualifies an entire sentence. Here is an comparison
While there is a relationship between these two sentences, the first expresses in a clear way that the intent is to enforce security. The second merely explains that security is available to everyone. These are not the same logic.

text:
14.1 LIE: Language, Introduction, & Elimination
One of the giants of 20th century logic, Alfred Tarski, gave an account of “What are Logical Notions?” His answer considered how these ideas evolved in history which lead him to a brilliant start of an answer.
Tarski used an example of his predecessor Klein. Imagine you are in high-school geometry, Euclid’s world, what might you say about the three triangles?
You might recall that triangles A and C are called congruent because they have the same angles and edge lengths. Euclid considered them the same. In fact much of Euclidean geometry is about making congruent copies of shapes with a ruler and compass. But of course there are differences. \(A\) is on the left, \(C\) is on the right. \(A\)’s right-angle is up, \(C\)’s right angle points down. Those differences are ones that abstraction to Euclid’s world simply ignores. Euclid’s abstraction is thus invariant (unchanging) to translation, rotations, and flips. All aspects of a diagram that are invariant to those transformations are the logic of Euclid’s geometry.
We can change the level of abstraction. We could insist for instance that the triangles not be rotated or flipped, only translations are allowed. That would make \(A\) no longer the same as \(C\). We would have lowered the level of abstraction being more precise about the differences. We can also go the other direction and raise the level of abstraction by ignoring the lengths of edges and comparing only interior angles, what are called similar triangles. Now the triangles \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) are all similar. This is a new world in which we can also rescale and ignore those transformations. Both directions have new logical notions.
We can push this further by permitting even more transformations, such as the option to move points around so long as we do not disconnect any shapes. That is, we care that a triangle has 3 vertices and 3 edges but we no longer care what lengths an angle mean. Those are known as continuous transformations and the resulting logic is called topology. In this world all three triangles are the same. (Using a different perspective we can proceed to abstract to graph theory and possibly other abtractions as well.)
Now Tarski’s goal was to imagine that we could keep raising the level of abstraction and at each level talk of logical notion. Tarski and many other logicians have suggested this process has to stop, and wherever it stops that is the most logical you can get.
The bottom for Tarski was something called Principia Mathematica, a book by Russell and Whitehead that tried to give foundation for math. It supports a number of useful logical notions: “and”, “if this then that”, “or”, “not”, and “true” and “false” are among them.
Recent researchers Andre Joyal and Jacob Lurie have argued instead that logic can always be refined to show more details so that there is no absolute bottom but instead categories of abstraction go on forever, Higher Topos Theories. Doing this dislodges “Principia” as the natural center and accordingly theorist are drifting into other foundations. We still can agree historically Prinicpia has a right to be mentioned near the center.
The English word “AND” is a bit too generic to make a reliable logical operator. For instance, we might write
In the first sentence 12 is given two properties that happen to coexist. This is the way logic thinks of “and”. Meanwhile the second sentence seems to indicate that the first property (studying) is responsible for the second (good grades). If you need further confirmation that something is different about these two uses consider swapping the order.
Be aware that logic steps back the options for the meaning of everyday words so that when used confusion is minimized.
In order to introduce logical operators recall from your childhood the notations used for other operators such as addition and multiplication:
\[
\begin{array}{rc}
  & 11\\
  + & 12\\
\hline
  & 23
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rc}
  & 11\\
  * & 12\\
\hline
  & 132
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rc}
\\
-  & 11\\
\hline
   & -11
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rc}
  & \\
0 & \\
\hline
  & 0
\end{array}
\] These last two are not too common but they continue the pattern showing that we could operate by the negative sign on a single input and the the constant 0 is akin to an operator with no inputs. We will use a similar notation to begin explaining our logical operators and later we will adjust this into what is known as “sequent calculus”. When this takes up too much vertical space we can flip the notation horizontally similar to \(11+12=23\), but instead of and \(=\) sign we use our judgment symbols \(P, Q\vdash R\) for example.
It may surprise you to notice that the LIE for AND we just used does specify what form of judgement we are using. AND so described could be used in all the styles of logic we have seen: Computational, Theoretical, or Practical. There is a similar logical operator available to nearly all logics called “implication”, but you may know it as “if…then”. We will explore that next.
It is convenient to include values as logical operators such as “true” or “false”.
Writing \(\top, P,\vdash P\) amounts to saying “if truth and P are valid then P is valid”. Some models of logic make \(P\vdash P\) a separate assumption called the Law of Identity.
The operator \(\neg P\), called negation is the composite \(P\to \bot\), \[
\tag{Negation}
\neg P := P\to \bot

title: 14   Fully structural Logical Operators
text:
To create a logical operator we need to specify three things:

Language: the symbols and grammar to be used to express the logical operator.
Introduction: what we need in place to create an instance of the logical operator.
Elimination: what we need in place along with context to use a logical operator.

Throughout this book we use the acronym LIE to remember these three components of a logical operator. Allow yourself to smirk win you turn in a “LIE” as part of your homework.



12 is positive and even
Study and you will get good grades.



12 is even and positive
You will get good grades and study.






Language: \(\wedge\) (“wedge” but pronounced “and”) is used to represent the logical operator “and”. The grammar for “and” is given by the following production rule: \[
\tag{$L_{\wedge}$}
\langle conjunction \rangle ::= \langle proposition \rangle \wedge \langle proposition \rangle
\]
Introduction: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are judged as valid then so is \(P\wedge Q\). In symbols \[
  \tag{$I_{\wedge}$}
  \begin{array}{rc}
   & P\\
  \wedge  &  Q\\
  \hline
  & P \wedge Q
  \end{array}
  \]
Elimination: If \(P\wedge Q\) is judged as valid then so are \(P\) and \(Q\). In symbols we want to remove the wedge and one side of the formula, so we think of this as subtraction type step which we denote by \(\wedge -\) to remove the right term and \(-\wedge\) to remove the left term. Worse notations have been invented, wait until you read the example from Lisp. \[
  \tag{$E_{\wedge}$}
  \begin{array}{rc}
   \wedge -   & P \wedge Q\\
  \hline
  & P
  \end{array}
  \qquad
  \begin{array}{rc}
   -\wedge   & P \wedge Q\\
  \hline
  & Q
  \end{array}
  \]





Language: \(\to\) (“arrow” but pronounced “implies”) is used to represent the logical operator “implies”. The grammar for “implies” is given by the following production rule: \[
\tag{$L_{\to}$}
\langle implication \rangle ::= \langle proposition \rangle \to \langle proposition \rangle
\]
Introduction: If \(P\) and \(Q\) are judged as valid then so is \(P\to Q\). In symbols \[
  \tag{$I_{\to}$}
  \begin{array}{rc}
\to   & P\vdash Q\\
  \hline
  & P \to Q
  \end{array}
  \]
Elimination: If \(P\to Q\) is judged as valid then so is \(Q\) if \(P\) is also judged as valid. In symbols \[
  \tag{$E_{\to}$}
  \begin{array}{rr}
   & P\to Q\\ @ & P\phantom{\to Q}   \\
  \hline
  & Q
  \end{array}
  \]

The elimination rule for \(\to\) is so famous it has its own name in Latin: “Modus Ponens”. Within classical mathematics the use of \(\Rightarrow\) is preferred to \(\to\) but that trend is changing as new forms of judgment take a larger role within mathematics.







NoteWhy \(\to\) versus \(\vdash\)?



The introduction of \(P\to Q\) by \(P\vdash Q\) is may seem like mere renaming. However, \(P\vdash Q\) is a statement of truth about our world and \(P\to Q\) is a proposition within the world. In fact we can write \(P\to Q\) even if it turns out to be false. However, similar to replacing the false proposition \(5=7\) with the obvious notation \(5\neq 7\), whenever we know \(P\to Q\) is false we make that clear with \(P\not\to Q\), and when we are uncertain if \(P\to Q\) is valid we says so in the surrounding text.




In Brouwerian logic we take truth to be a symbol from which is judged valid from any we start any

Language: \(\top\) (“top” but pronounced “true”), also denoted true or 1 in software. The grammar for \(\top\) is \[
\tag{$L_{\top}$}
\langle truth \rangle ::= \top
\]
Introduction: \(\top\) is always valid, depending on nothing. In symbols \[
\tag{$I_{\top}$}
\overline{\top}\qquad \text{ i.e. }\vdash \top
\]
Elimination: \(\top\) leads to every valid proposition \(P\). In symbols, \[
\tag{$E_{\top}$}
\begin{array}{rc}
    & \top\\
    & P\\
  \hline
   & P
  \end{array}
  \qquad \text{ i.e. }\top,P \vdash P
\]




In many systems of judgment we want to avoid any inconsistences. Nothing can be both true and false. This lead some systems to assume a false that is quite difficult to

Introduction: None! We don’t want to allow our logic to introduce falsehoods.

\text{P is a proposition}, \bot \vdash P
\]

Recall on our earlier discussion of Brouwerian verification judgments we insisted every valid propositions \(P\) had to be derivable from truth, so \(\top,P\to P\) hypothesis that \(P\) is valid (along with \(\top\) which by its introduction is always valid) and it derives \(P\). Suppose you are told \(P\to \bot\) is valid. What does this say about \(P\)? Show that \[

\]



Naming operators
Once we create operators we try to give them names that resemble their use in natural language but as we have seen judgment changes from computational, theoretical, and practical. This means that the meanings of our operator drift. However, to keep some sense of continuity we often find that the language and grammar are kept the same and keep either the introduction or the elimination rule the same. When we keep the introduction rules the same we refer to the operators as “covariant” and when keep the elimination rule the same we refer to it as “contravariant”. This name comes from the associated diagrams.

14.3 A diagram view of “And”
As our above proof shows we often can get some impact from a diagram view of logical operators. This can help to point out some details that are missing.

Diagram for introduction rules
Let us consider why we come to know \(P\) and \(Q\) are valid when we write the introduction rule for \(\wedge\). Surely everything occurs in a context, let us call this \(\Gamma\). Putting the two together means that one even has occured that lead you to believe in both at the same stage of your argument. Let us put that reason into the notation. \[
\tag{$I'_{\wedge}$}
\begin{array}{crcl}
    & \Gamma, R & \vdash & P\\
\wedge &   \Gamma, S & \vdash & Q\\
\hline
    & \Gamma, R\wedge S & \vdash & P \wedge Q
\end{array}
\] To draw thus we can resort to comic strips where we draw separate panels that we can read together as an evolving story. In the first panel we have the reason \(R\) that leads to \(P\) through evidence \(f\) and the reason \(S\) that leads to \(Q\) from evidence \(g\). In the second panel we have the conjunction of the reasons \(R\wedge S\) that lead to the conjunction of the propositions \(P\wedge Q\). To make the diagrams we may as well replace \(A\vdash B\) with \(A\to B\) since it makes the diagram look familiar. For \(\Gamma\) we shade the background to indicate that it is a context that is always present everything takes place within it.
flowchart LR
    subgraph panel1["Context Γ"]
        direction LR
        R["Prop R"] -->|f| P["Prop P"]
        S["Prop S"] -->|g| Q["Prop Q"]
    end
    subgraph panel2["Context Γ after Conjunction"]
        direction LR
        R1["Prop R"] -->|f| P1["Prop P"]
        RS["Prop R ∧ S"] -->|I'<sub>∧</sub>| PQ["Prop P ∧ Q"]
        S1["Prop S"] -->|g| Q1["Prop Q"]
        style RS fill:#55ff55,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
        style PQ fill:#55ff55,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    end

    linkStyle 5 stroke:transparent,fill:transparent
    
    style panel1 fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style panel2 fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    
The elimination rules now start from the position of knowing \(P\wedge Q\) is valid for some reason and extracting just the validity of \(P\) or \(Q\). \[
\frac{
    \Gamma \vdash P \wedge Q
}{
    \Gamma \vdash P
}(E_{\wedge -})
\qquad
\frac{
    \Gamma \vdash P \wedge Q
}{
    \Gamma \vdash Q
}(E_{-\wedge})
\] Now when we diagram this we realize we also get similar rules from \(R\wedge S\). So when we put these together we get the following final diagram.
flowchart LR
    subgraph panel["Context Γ Conjunction"]
        direction LR
        R["Prop R"] -->|f| P["Prop P"]
        RS["Prop R ∧ S"] -->|I'<sub>∧</sub>| PQ["Prop P ∧ Q"]
        RS -->|E<sub>-∧</sub><sup>R</sup>| R["Prop R"]
        RS -->|E<sub>∧-</sub><sup>S</sup>| S["Prop S"]
        PQ -->|E<sub>-∧</sub><sup>P</sup>| P["Prop P"]
        PQ -->|E<sub>∧-</sub><sup>Q</sup>| Q["Prop Q"]
        S["Prop S"] -->|g| Q["Prop Q"]

        style PQ fill:#55ff55,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    end
    style panel fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
To make this diagram even more powerful let us observe that if we follow arrows two different ways and get to the same place, the results are equal. For example, \[
\begin{aligned}
f \text{ after } E_{\wedge -}^{R} & = E_{\wedge -}^{P} \text{ after } I'_{\wedge}\\
f \text{ after } E_{-\wedge}^{R} & = E_{-\wedge}^{P} \text{ after } I'_{\wedge}
\end{aligned}
\] This concept has a name.

A commutative diagram is a diagram of arrows such that any two oriented paths that start and end at the same place are considered equal.

Now we see something much more nuanced, for instance this captures how we may need to behave when dealing shared resources since we keep as many reason in the premise as uses in the conclusion.






NoteOrder of operations



A lot of grammar is tedious to read with extra parenthesis. To avoid this mathematicians prefer to teach an order of operations rule (which is entirely arbitrary but agreed to by community).

Parenthesis overrule everything.
Read operators left to right, so \(P\to Q\to R\) reads as \(P\to (Q\to R)\) not \((P\to Q)\to R\).
And \(\wedge\) is stronger than \(\to\) so \(P\wedge Q\to R\) means \((P\wedge Q)\to R\) not \(P\wedge (Q\to R)\).



When in doubt, use parenthesis to make your meaning clear.






TipIdentifying introduction and elimination rules



In a diagram that specifies the result \(R\) of logical operators then

the introduction rules are those that have arrows pointing into \(R\).
the elimination rules are those that have arrows pointing out of \(R\).

(5 mins) Overview
The last of the inductive logics we will pursue are gathered under two general names:

Abductive Reasoning: deciding what is plausible.
Probabilistic Reasoning: assigning a measurement to outcomes.


Abductive Reasoning
Abductive reasoning is most commonly practiced in investigations, for example, it is plausible given the evidence that so-and-so happened. This can be applied everywhere from in law practices, to medicine, and to scientific experiments. Stated logically, it is the process of guessing the missing context that would validate the claims. That is, given evidence (E), some established theory (T), make some hypothetical assumptions (H) such that



LaTeX: T, H E


Notice in contrast when we had deductive reasoning we had all the elements to the left of the turnstile () and wanted to conclude the values on the right. So if deduction is like calculating, e.g. (2+3=?), then abduction. is a way solving for an unknown, e.g. (2+x=5), what is (x)?

What’s with the name?
Abduct is a word most of us hear in negative stations, someone is taken away against their will, or a person of authority leaves their post unattended. The philosophy Charles Peirce coined the term for logical purposes possibly influenced by how it sounds in comparison to induction and deduction and because it meaning “to lead away” could be understood as how learning what is plausible is often a fight not to be mislead. It is a settled term today in any case.
As a general remark, some logicians treat abduction as separate from induction form a third in the list of deduction, induction, abduction. Our own definition of induction is to reason beyond the evidence and therefore include abduction. Whether we treat abduction as a subset of induction or as a separate style of reasoning is not too consequential. Just be aware that authors differ on this topic.



Probabilistic Reasoning
Probability assigns a number to events as a way of (hopefully) quantifying why events happen the way the see them happen. If we flip a coin we expect a heads as often as a tail. We therefore do not find it unfair to choose which team begins a match with the ball based on a coin toss. But if instead choose the starting team by flipping a pencil to see if lands on the side or on the tip, suddenly we would think it unfair to one of the teams because in our experience it is astronomically unlikely that a pencil will ever land on anything but its side. Probability seeks to put a number to that experience so that we can easily explain why coin flip events are so different from pencil flip events.

Is it rational?
Mathematicians are drawn mostly to the probabilistic side of reasoning because it puts numbers in our hands and with that a great many mathematical tools become available. Even so, when pressed to explain the justifications of putting numbers to events we are often forced to confront a form of abductive reasoning as justification. In our final unit we will preview two the dueling philosophies of probability (frequentist and Bayesian). The existences of an open debate is a sign of the youth of probability as a subject. Many of its main tools were invented in the past century and its logical footing is shifting as well. It is an exciting time to join the subject.



Objectives

Recognize and describe differences between Abductive & Probabilistic Logic
Observe and discuss distribution, uniform distribution versus Gaussian Distribution
Compute with conditional probability.
Analyze Monte Carlo and Las Vegas Algorihtms

title: 27  Inductive Reasoning
text:
27.1 Where do we use Inductive Logic?
We are now launching our second of three major units on reasoning. So far we have focussed on
Deductive Logic: reasoning from the evidence provided.
Now we will focus on a much more realistic but nuanced form of reasoning where we have incomplete evidence and still need to make logical decisions.
Inductive Logic: reasoning beyond the evidence provided.
If you read the definition “reason beyond the evidence” you might begin to worry if this is scientific, certainly it would seem dubious as mathematics which tries to be completely proof based. But what if you attempt to read a complex math formula like the following one.
\[
\frac{\left(\sqrt{9-x^2}\right)(x-18)}{1-x+2x^2-4x^3+8?}
\]
For most of use this formula will be too long to absorb all at once. Instead we are very likely to begin to read it from top-to-bottom, left-to-right under the hypothesis that it will indeed reveal itself as a complete mathematical formula. When we read the numerator we don’t yet have the evidence that the denominator will be a math formula. We are reasoning beyond our evidence. And in fact it is only when we get to the very end that we find in disappointment that it was not a standard math formula because it had a stray typo, an ? that should probably have been something else. But look back, was this any less “logical” to proceed under a hypothesis that we had a formula? Probably not. We can imagine that most of the time we don’t encounter flaws and this induction—reasoning beyond the evidence—was every bit as “logical” as our examples of deductive logic.

title: 30  Relations and Order
text:
30.1 General Relations
We saw with deduction that one of the ways to build a new data type is to modify what we mean by “equals”. In programs we override equality. But you are likely familiar with other ways we relate data. For example, some numbers are large, others are small, that means \(x\leq y\). Likewise some expressions in reasoning benefit from organization.
To turn data like 541 or a PDF into a value we can judge we need to create a relation. Here are some samples relations.
crumbs: VI. Relations
30  Relations and Order

title: 30  Relations and Order
text:
P(541) = “541 is positive”. Something we can judge, and we judge it is true.
P(541) = “541 is even.” Something we can also judge, but this time we judge it is false.
Q(MyCV.pdf) = “MyCV.pdf has page numbers.” Something we can judge. Is it true? We’d have to read the file to find out.


Propositions
A Proposition is a sentence we can claim and judge. The outcome depends on our mode. Recall from Week 1 we have three forms of propositions

\(\text{Prop}\) for Theory is generally True \(\top\) and False \(\bot\)
\(\text{Prop}\) for Computation is generally True \(\top\) and False \(\bot\) but must be supported by evidence so it may not come to an end if the evidence never comes.
\(\text{Prop}\) for Practice is generally True \(\top\), False \(\bot\) along with a host of gray are, perhaps Maybe, or Unknown, or Likely, Unlikely, etc. We will here simplify and just allow a single third value +.


Relations
So what is a Relation? First choose the appropriate proposition category (Theory, Computation, or Practice). Then a Relation is a function form lists of types \(X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n\) into \(\text{Prop}\). That is
\(P:X_1\times \cdots \times X_n\to \text{Prop}\)

P(x) = “x is positive”. This is not something we can judge yet, but as soon as we replace the variable by a value we will be able to judge it. In fact this sort of claim is simply true of false, Theory proposition applies.. So this is a function from data into propositions but it only makes sense when given decimal numbers \(\mathbb{R}\). It is a Relation \(P:\mathbb{R}\to \{\top,\bot\}\)
P(x,y) = “x +y =0”. This is a either true or false, so we can judge this once given decimal numbers of x and y so this is a relation \(P:\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\to \{\top,\bot\}\)
Q(x) = “x has page numbers”. Here x is a file, so File is our input type. However, the concept of “has page number” is clear for documents but it means nothing for images, videos and so many other documents. This suggests a practical proposition of Prop={true, false, undefined}. This is a relation \(Q: \text{File} -> \{\text{true, false, undefined}\}\). In common software syntax this might be def hasPageNumbers(x : File) : Option[Boolean]. The Option wrapper allows us to give back a value of True/False when it makes sense, or nothing when the input file is not a document.




General Relation Vocabulary

Valence or Arity is the number of inputs to a relation. E.g. P(x), Q(x) are valence 1, also called unary. P(x,y) is binary, valence 2.
Homogeneous: a relation \(R:X_1\times \cdots\times X_n\to \text{Prop}\) where for each \(i,j\), \(X_i=X_j\). In this case we often write \(R:X^n\to \text{Prop}\).
Heterogenous: a relation that may not be homogeneous. In general a homogeneous relation is also heterogenous but not the other way around.

Mathematical Conventions
Mathematics tends to study relations \(R:X_1\times \cdots \times X_n\to \text{Prop}\) more fully than other subjects and much of mathematics is in the Theory camp of reasoning. Because of this most of mathematics sees relations as just true and false. When this is the case then it is enough to know just the values which are true.
\(\{(x_1,\ldots, x_n)\in X_1\times \cdots \times X_n \mid \Gamma \vdash R(x_1,\ldots, x_n) \}\)
Because of this, much of mathematics will define relations not by a function but by a subset, that is, mathematics will often write
\(R\subset X_1\times \cdots \times X_n\)
Even if this is bit short cited on the part of mathematicians not to consider the nuance of relations in computation and in practice, it is still a notation used broadly and you can introduce that notation meaning in fact \(R:X_1\times \cdots \times X_n\to \text{Prop}\). Just add that clarity to your discussion in text.

title: 30  Relations and Order
text:
30.2 Binary Homogeneous Relations
Amongst the most used relations are binary homogeneous relations
\(R:X\times X\to \text{Prop}\)
In this case we generally prefer an infix notation. Example, instead of \(R(x,y)\) we choose some symbol, maybe = or < or == etc. and write things like
\(x=y\), \(x<y\), x==y, x!=y, \(x\subset y\)
Since we need to keep talking about many binary homogeneous relations we will continue to use R as a generic name
\(xRy\)

Reflexive law
A binary homogeneous relation \(R:X^2\to \text{Prop}\) is called reflexive if
\(\forall x.(xRx)\)

In number equality is reflexive \(x=x\), less than is not reflexive \(5<5\) is false, but less-than or equal is reflexive \(x\leq x\)
In programming if one data type B extends another A it means every method for A is a method for B as well, though B may have further methods. Under this definition A has all the methods that A has so A extends A. However, in writing a program you may not be allowed to write A extends A as that leads the programming language to get confused with circular reasoning. This is a difference in definitions, so even experts can disagree on this one with good reason.
A daughter inherits traits from her father, but a daughter does not inherit traits from herself. So inheritence is not generally reflexive.

30.3 Reflexive Closure
In some situations it is convenient to assume a relation is reflexive even if it is not. Think of promoting \(x<y\) into \(x\leq y\). This literally means
\(x\leq y \qquad := (x=x) \vee (x<y)\)
We can do this to absolutely any binary homogeneous relation \(R:X^2\to \text{Prop}\)
\(x\leq y \qquad := (x=x) \vee (x<y)\)
The resulting relation \(R^=\) is called the reflexive closure. The notation we usually use is to add part of the equal sign to the original symbol. Here are some examples

\(< \leadsto \leq\)
\(\subset \leadsto \subseteq\)

In other situations we want to remove reflexivity. We can do this as well.
\(x\lneq y \qquad := (x\neq x) \wedge (x\leq y)\)
The notation similarly strikes out the equal portion.

Definition. A homogeneous binary relation \(R:X^2\to \text{Prop}\) is called an order relation if it is transitive. It is furthermore

title: 34  Using Adaptive Logic
text:
34.1 Overview
The point of an adaptive logic for computation is to put a formal system of reasoning around various situations in computing that may fail in unpredictable ways, but are also somewhat common occurrences. The loose plan is to create two logics, one stronger than the other. The weaker logic represents the actual computation, and the stronger logic is like a virtual machine running within our systems with its ideal rules. When the ideal rules break, the weaker logic takes over.

title: 34  Using Adaptive Logic
text:
34.2 A Scenario of Abnormalities
Let’s look into one scenario where we model the behavior of closing an application.

Designed behavior
First lets look at the design goal. You have an application where users can create some data. You have the following design goal:When a user closes the app with unsaved work, the app should put up a warning telling them to go back and save the work, or delete it and continue closing. In symbols:

(U) = “There exists unsaved work”
(C) = “Close application”; hence, (C) = “Do not close application”.
(D) = “Delete unsaved work.”

The rule given is that necessarily (U) and possibly (C) leads to ((C)) or (D). More precisely((U)( C) (C)D)

Technical Remark. We are using qualifiers “necessary” () and “possibly” () to clarify the subtle point that closing is a process over time. If we strip these away and write(UC (C)D)it would read as saying that (C) is true, i.e. (UC C) is one of the elimination rules of an AND. So that would seem to immediately remove even the option not to close, which we actually want our user to have. By using “possibly C” ((C)), we are chasing down the scenario where it is possible to have (C) or (C). Given that we put in qualifiers it makes sense also to require that there actually be unsaved work before warning the user about loosing it; hence, (U).In reality the better qualifiers are from temporal modal logic that are better suited at describing knowledge over time. As we are not studying such logics we leave this as a hint that if you continue in this direction there are many resources to help.



Race / Deadlock Scenario

Event A global resource warning prompts you to shut apps down. In haste, you attempt to close an app with unsaved work. You see the warning dialog and click Abort (intending (C)). Meanwhile, the system begins shutting apps down automatically (forcing (C)).
Result The system enters a confused state where both (C) and (C) are active (e.g., competing threads: one closing, one restoring).

Formally, we have:(C(C))Now, classically, this shouldn’t be possible, and it is not in our classical theoretical logic. But reality trumps theory. From the perspective of the program we are best able to explain the current situation as a logic that allows such contradictions. (Perhaps a 3 valued logic like a paraconsistent logic).

title: 34  Using Adaptive Logic
text:
34.3 Modeling the Problem
Having a logic that allows for inconsistency does not mean to give up on reasoning, rather it allows us to embrace fixes and clarifications that don’t seek to diagnose the inscrutable circumstances that got us here but rather focus on what to do next. Let us write down precise differences in our classical expectation and what it is we actually witnessed.

Upper Logic
Classical logic would push toward resolution via Disjunctive Syllogism (()):(())implying the system should delete the unsaved work and proceed to close. Let’s call this the Upper Logic UL, which is the logic we think should be there.


Lower Logic
But in reality, the system hung due to a race/deadlock (two threads enforcing (C) and (C)). The contradiction persists instead of resolving. At a lower level we have a logic where () is not validated. Instead we have much more boring derivation that requires no special rules at all.(())We call this a fact because you can prove this any logic that Ands (()), Ors (()), and Nots (()). All we are saying is that EITHER we delete the unsaved work and continue, or else we are in a confused state of ((C C)). Let’s call this the Lower Logic LL, which is the logic we actually have.


Abnormalities
We can treat (C(C)) as an abnormality (Ab()) triggered by data () (e.g. running out of memory and entering an emergency shutdown). Now we can return to the classical rule and describe it as n Conditional Rule (CR) meaning it depends on not having the abnormality (Ab()).(C,  (C)D {CL} D C,  (C)D {CL} D Ab())We would say simply that (C, (C)D _{CL} D) is “Conditional Rule”, conditioned on the data (). As long as we avoid the abnormality (Ab()) we have the intended behavior. Rules in the lower logic LL are by design always Unconditional Rules (UR).


Summary of the Model
What have we achieved? We have managed to create an underpinning of logic where the behavior we are witnessing is not illogical. It is merely what this logic allows. And because of this we can now design a logical step to follow this. Ideally we fix the “problem” – i.e. the case (C(C)) which doesn’t fit our intended classical expectation.
crumbs: VII. Default and Adaptive Logic
34  Using Adaptive Logic

title: 34  Using Adaptive Logic
text:
34.4 Fixing the problem
Having a lower logic that accurately separate the abnormal behavior, if they occur we no exactly problem to try to address. Unlike default logic, where one rule overrides another in cases of confusion, we do not need to know precisely how created the abnormality. We simply observe that it occurred and proceed with a logic to handle that scenario. For example, it might be that in a confused state the data the user has is also corrupted and could cause harm to our system if not removed. We might therefore proceed with a rule that deletes all user data hasn’t been saved. (E.g. removing all temporary files.).((CC)D())Or perhaps we know this application space is safe and we have other means to protect against errors so even a partially save project might be reconstructed from temporary files when the application is restarted. So we might purposefully save all temporary files overriding any user decisions.((CC)D())Whatever the design choices, we now have a system of logic to express logical outcomes in the face of inconsistent data.

The catch
The one obstacle is that if we proceed with conditional rules only to find conclusions that are eventually abnormal, then we leave behind inconclusive logic. So what we maintain is a rule that as prove our steps we leave a mark next to any claim which is later invalidated by an abnormality. This means that ever step in our proof maintains an ongoing list of possible abnormalities. If any should occur we search back wards and invalid (mark) all rules that are conditioned on that abnormality. Those no longer count towards the reasoning leaving behind a completely logic progression of step, if only in retrospect. The precise mechanics of back tracking could seem to take a long time to search. But there is a weapon in the programmer’s arsenal called “dynamic programming” (or memorization) which in effects reuses previously made calculations and behaves much more efficiently. You can study those details in a future algorithms class. For now, we simply apply in our specific examples.

title: 34  Using Adaptive Logic
text:
34.5 Revisiting the Scenario
Let us imagine that we take the pessimistic solution. We are running several apps at once when our computer tells us it is dangerously low on memory and recommends we close applications. We panic and start closing application, one of them having unsaved work which triggers the warning. We click to abort the close so we can save the file, but by this point the operating system is in emergency mode and sending mandatory close calls to all apps. We enter an abnormality of (CC). This violates Conditional Rule and drops our app out of the hypothetical classical logic into the real world with inconsistencies. Then locating the pessimistic rule, we delete all the user data. Miraculously it was actually one of our temporary files that was growing in size and causing the problem in the first place. Having just deleted it, the system recovers and goes back to functioning normally. Crisis averted, some user data lost.

Let us work out the formal adaptive logic table for this scenario using the following propositions: Defined Propositions:

(U) = “There exists unsaved work”
(C) = “Close application”
(D) = “Delete unsaved work”

Additional Propositions:

(E) = “Emergency system shutdown initiated”
(Ab()) = “Abnormality: ((C C))” where () represents the race condition data

Rules:

CR1 (Conditional): (U C (C D)) [Standard close behavior - conditional on no abnormality] Abnromality (Ab()=C(C)) when () is some complex race condition.
(Unconditional): (M E C) [Emergency close - always applies]
(Unconditional): (U C ((C C) D)) [Lower logic reality]
(Pessimistic Rule): ((C C) D) [Abnormality resolution]

StepFormulaRule AppliedStatusNotes
1(M)Premise✓ ValidMemory warning occurs
2(U)Premise✓ ValidUnsaved work exists
3(E)From 1✓ ValidSystem enters emergency mode
4(C)From 1,3 by UR1✓ ValidEmergency close initiated
5(C)User attempts abort✓ ValidUser clicks abort

Adaptive Backtracking.

Step 6 is made by CR1, but initially conditional on the absence of the abnormality (Ab()).
Step 7 triggers the abnormality (Ab()) which marks 6 and removes it from further consideration.
The valid logical thus now skips 6 and goes (1).
So in the end, the pessimistic rule takes over and deletes the file.

This table demonstrates how adaptive logic handles the contradiction by:

Detecting abnormalities when classical logic fails
Marking invalid steps that depended on violated conditions
Applying specialized rules (PR) to resolve abnormal states
Maintaining logical consistency through retrospective validation

Once we settle on a form of judgment, be it computational \(\vdash\), practical \(\Vdash\), or theoretical \(\vDash\), we now have to ask what we want to judge. It was here that the logician Charles Sanders Peirce (1839-1914) laid out a spectrum.

Abductive Reasoning: to find the best hypothesis for the evidence.

text:
33.2 Defeasible judgement
A judgement \(A\vdash B\) is called defeasible, denoted \(A\overset{D}{\vdash} B\) if the addition of some judgements \(C\) may lead to invalidating it \(C,A\nvdash B\). We can capture this as a modal condition
\[
A\overset{D}{\vdash} B \qquad \equiv\qquad (A\vdash B)\wedge \big(\diamond \big( \exists C. (C,A\nvdash B)\big)\big)
\]
Do not worry about the symbols if they don’t help you. You can break it down by saying

You much have A leading to B, and
It is possible to add further evidence C where C together with A no longer leads to B.

The propositions “C” that occur in a defeasible judgement are called defeaters. Identifying defeaters is a mix of common sense and subject matter expertise.

A common sense defeater

You click on the image file leading to it being displayed in the browser.
A=“You click on the image file”
B=“It is displayed in the browser”
Together \(A\vdash B\)
It is possible that the image type is not supported by the browser.
C=“Image type is not supported”. (A defeater)
Together \(A,C\nvdash B\)

Therefore \(A\vdash B\) and \(\diamond (\exists C)(A,C\nvdash b\). So \(A\overset{D}{\vdash} B\) is a defeasible proposition..

In this example it is likely that common sense convinces you that “C=Image not supported” would defeat the rules. But in the following example it would only be someone with specific knowledge that could inform us about the defeaters.


A expert dependent defeater
Consider the following three

A = The container is bowl shaped.
B = The container holds liquids.
C = The liquid is helium.

Our common sense will tell use that \(A\vdash B\), e.g. water is help in a bowl, oil is held in a bowl, and so one. This is a sound judgement. However, an expert in low-temperature superfluids would be able to inform us that liquid helium exhibit zero-viscosity and therefore has no friction the side of the bowl and will creep up the sides and pour over the edges. This defeats the claim and so \(A\overset{D}{\vdash}B\). Of course this could only be expressed to us through a subject matter expert as our daily experiences do not encounter liquid helium.
Alfred Leitner, 1963, Public Domain.


Was the first entailment just wrong?
When we first deal with default logic from the lens of deductive reasoning it is tempting to want to revisit the initial entailment \(A\vdash B\) and claim this was in error. There are at least two responses to give to this feeling. First of all, humans built logic and did so in the hopes of solving their problems. So if default logic makes for easier reasoning on some problems we should not be shy to use it even if it is not the right tool for some other applications. The second response is that if we think long enough there is very little outside of formal mathematics which would ever deserve the judgement \(A\vdash B\) because nearly every claim we will make will be couched in some default assumptions often unspoken and too difficult to uncover. So in a practical sense we would get nothing done if we insisted on beginning without defaults. Thus if we are making a specification of a program and want to explain a feature as
“You click on the image leading to the image displaying in the browser”
We are not behaving irrationally. We are merely lacking the later specificity that will unpack this discussion. And it gives us a compact digestible goal to begin aiming at.
And in case you think this is a choice only faced by practical sciences just take a look at the question of solving \(x^2-2=0\). I natural default is to assume that \(x=\pm \sqrt{2}\) is two solutions. That is until you meet a subject matter expert who wants numbers to represent binary values modulo 2. Defaults are natural, embrace them and your reasoning will be easier on others.

text:
27.2 Where is inductive logic in computation?
Much of the data we make or use is complex which literally means it is made out of parts, like a building complex that has several smaller buildings linked together. An example of this is JSON blob that stores social network data as a mix of GPS coordinates, text messages, images, id numbers and much more. Reasoning about complex data doesn’t have to be “complex”, as in “complicated”, but it does benefit from a strategy. The strategy that logic attaches to the study of complex data is known as induction. What it means in this case is that we do not try to understand the entire JSON blob all at once. Instead we learn a series of simpler rules to reason locally under the assumption that when we see the whole data it will make sense. At any one stage we are forced to “reason beyond the evidence we have”. In retrospect the logic we have seen up to this point should be known as deductive. Induction comes from the word “induce” and the idea of induction is to study complex events as mix of smaller evidence that that induce us towards an understanding of the whole.
